title: Babies or Believers? Why Christians Baptize Differently
excerpt: Christians agree that Christ commanded baptism and disagree about whether the children of believers should receive it. The disagreement is eighteen centuries old, each side has real texts, and it was once settled by drowning people.
body:
A grandmother watches her grandchildren grow up unbaptized and lies awake over it. In her church, baptism was the first thing done for a child, and she can't understand parents who would wait. A college student who was baptized as a baby comes to a living faith at nineteen and wants to be baptized, and his parents hear the request as a judgment on everything they did for him. A husband and wife from two different churches stand over a crib and realize they have never settled this. And a skeptic looks at all of them and asks how a religion can claim to know the mind of God when it can't agree on how to get people in the door.

Nobody in that paragraph is being foolish. Each one is holding something that matters. The trouble is that for most Christians the argument was inherited already finished. They know what their church does. Few have heard the other side's case from someone who believes it.

## What Every Christian Shares

It helps to see first how small the disputed ground is. All Christians baptize because Christ told them to: "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). All of them use water and that threefold name. All of them understand baptism as union with Christ in his death and resurrection, as Paul describes it: "We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life" (Romans 6:4). And all of them baptize adult converts on a profession of faith. A church that baptizes infants does not baptize an unbelieving grown man because his neighbors are Christians. It asks him what he believes.

So the question is narrower than it sounds. It concerns the children of believers. Should the sign be given to them at the beginning, with faith expected to follow, or held until they can speak for themselves? Behind that sits a second question, about how much water and how it is applied, which matters less and will come up along the way.

## The Texts

The New Testament has no sentence that settles it. It never records the baptism of a baby, and it never forbids one. It also never shows the child of Christian parents growing up and being baptized later. Almost everyone baptized in its pages is a first-generation convert.

What it does have are texts that each side reads with some confidence. At Pentecost Peter says, "Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins," and then, "For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself" (Acts 2:38–39). One side hears the order of the first sentence: repent, then be baptized. The other hears the reach of the second: you and your children.

Three times a whole household is baptized. Lydia "was baptized, and her household as well" (Acts 16:15). The jailer in Philippi "was baptized at once, he and all his family" (Acts 16:33). Paul mentions that he baptized "the household of Stephanas" (1 Corinthians 1:16). No ages are given. One side notes that an ancient household ordinarily included children and that the head's faith brought the whole house with it. The other notes that Luke goes on to say the jailer "rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God" (Acts 16:34), which sounds like people old enough to rejoice.

Paul ties baptism to circumcision in one dense sentence. Believers have received "a circumcision made without hands," he says, "having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God" (Colossians 2:11–12). One side sees the old sign of the covenant, which was given to eight-day-old boys, answered by a new one. The other points to the words "through faith." And Peter says that baptism "now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ" (1 Peter 3:21). A sentence that says baptism saves and in the same breath calls it "an appeal to God" has been claimed, reasonably, by everybody.

## The First Centuries

The record after the apostles is thin at first, and both sides find themselves in it.

The oldest church manual we have, the Didache, is usually dated to around the year 100. Its instructions assume a candidate who can prepare. In the translation printed in the Ante-Nicene Fathers it says, "thou shalt order the baptized to fast one or two days before." It prefers running water and allows pouring where there is not enough. It says nothing about infants either way.

Around the year 200 the North African writer Tertullian discusses the baptism of small children directly, and he advises against it. Of children he writes, in S. Thelwall's translation, "let them become Christians when they have become able to know Christ." His reason is the seriousness of sins committed after baptism, and for the same reason he tells unmarried adults to wait as well. His advice shows two things at once. Children were being baptized by his time, or there would be nothing to object to. And a respected teacher could oppose the practice without being thought a heretic.

Half a century later the question in North Africa had moved on. A man named Fidus had argued that a baby should not be baptized before the eighth day, on the pattern of circumcision. Cyprian of Carthage answered for a council of sixty-six bishops that there was no reason to wait even that long: "we all rather judge that the mercy and grace of God is not to be refused to any one born of man."

Even then the practice wasn't uniform. Late in the fourth century Gregory of Nazianzus, preaching in Constantinople, told parents to baptize an infant at once if it was in danger of death, and otherwise gave his advice "to wait till the end of the third year, or a little more or less," when a child can answer a few questions. Augustine, whose mother was devout, was not baptized as a child. He writes in the *Confessions* that when he fell gravely ill as a boy his mother was ready to have him baptized, and that when he recovered, "my cleansing was deferred." He was baptized as a grown man. A generation later he was the great defender of baptizing infants.

Those who baptize infants read this history as continuity. No one in the early church, they point out, ever protests that infant baptism is a new invention. Tertullian argues that it is unwise, and he does not argue that it is unheard of. Those who baptize believers read the same history as a slow drift. The earliest evidence assumes instruction and fasting, the first clear witness objects, and delay was common in Christian families for another two hundred years.

## The Reformation, and the River

The question was reopened in Zurich. In 1525 some of the associates of the reformer Ulrich Zwingli concluded from the New Testament that baptism follows faith, and they baptized one another as adults. Their opponents called them Anabaptists, rebaptizers.

What followed is the church's guilt. In that century nearly every government in Europe, Catholic and Protestant, treated a second baptism as a crime against both church and public order, because in a society where every infant was baptized, to refuse was to step outside the community itself. In Zurich they met imprisonment, torture, banishment and death, and the city drowned Felix Manz, one of their leaders. Across Europe they were drowned, burned or beheaded. A violent uprising by one radical group in the city of Münster in the 1530s was then used to justify the killing of a peaceful majority who wanted only to follow their conscience.

Christians did this to Christians over the meaning of a sacrament of union. Jesus had warned that "the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God" (John 16:2). He was speaking of what would be done to his disciples. He did not say that his disciples would one day do it to one another.

## The Case for Baptizing the Children of Believers

Those who baptize the children of believers reason this way.

God has always dealt with his people as families. When he made his covenant with Abraham he promised "to be God to you and to your offspring after you" (Genesis 17:7), and he commanded that the sign of that covenant be given to infants. Paul calls that sign "a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith" (Romans 4:11). So a sign of faith was given, by God's command, to children who did not yet believe. The new covenant is wider and more generous than the old. It would be strange if at its opening the children of believers were put out of a place they had held for two thousand years, and stranger still if no Jewish Christian in the New Testament is recorded objecting. Peter's first sermon repeats the old formula, "for you and for your children." Jesus was indignant when children were kept from him and said that "to such belongs the kingdom of God" (Mark 10:14).

Beneath the texts is a conviction about grace. Baptism is first of all God's word to us and only then our word to him. An infant at the font, who contributes nothing and understands nothing, is the truest picture there is of how anyone is saved. Faith is expected to follow, and the child is raised to own the promise for himself. The Westminster Confession of 1647 puts the conclusion in a sentence: "Not only those that do actually profess faith in and obedience unto Christ, but also the infants of one or both believing parents are to be baptized." Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran Christians go further and hold that in baptism God actually gives the new birth of which Jesus spoke: "unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God" (John 3:5).

## The Case for Baptizing Believers Only

Those who baptize only believers reason this way.

Every baptism the New Testament describes in any detail follows the same order. People hear the gospel, believe it, and are baptized. "So those who received his word were baptized" (Acts 2:41). "When they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women" (Acts 8:12). The command of Jesus runs in that order too: make disciples, baptize them, teach them. The apostles describe baptism in terms that fit only a person who is acting. It is "an appeal to God for a good conscience." It is being raised with Christ "through faith." The household passages, read to the end, speak of households that heard the word and believed.

Beneath the texts is a conviction about the church. The prophets promised a new covenant unlike the old in exactly this respect: "they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest" (Jeremiah 31:34). Israel was a nation one entered by birth. The church is a people one enters by new birth, and Abraham's children are now those who share his faith: "if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring" (Galatians 3:29). To give the sign of that new birth to someone who has shown no evidence of it confuses the church with the families of its members. The Baptist confession written in London in 1677 puts the conclusion in a sentence: "Those who do actually professe repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience, to our Lord Jesus, are the only proper subjects of this ordinance." Most who hold this view also hold that the word baptize means to immerse, and that going under the water and coming up is the picture Paul has in mind in Romans 6.

## What Each Side Fears

Each side fears something real in the other, and each fear has come true somewhere.

Those who baptize believers fear a church full of people who were baptized, never converted, and assured all their lives that they were Christians. They look at centuries in which baptism and citizenship were the same thing and whole nations were counted as the church. That happened.

Those who baptize infants fear a faith that begins with the self. They see baptism turned into a testimony about a personal decision, children raised as outsiders in their own church until they can produce an experience, and a rebaptism that tells most of the Christians who have ever lived that their baptism was nothing. That has happened too.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

That Christ commanded baptism, that it is given with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and that it joins a person to the one church, belongs to the faith all Christians confess. So does the truth that salvation is God's gift in Christ.

Who should be baptized, and how, is a question of the second order. It is a serious one. A congregation has to do one thing or the other, which is why Christians who agree on nearly everything else worship in separate churches over it. But it has never been in the creeds. People on both sides hold the whole faith, and today most of them know it.

Paul wrote that there is "one Lord, one faith, one baptism" (Ephesians 4:5). Neither side can read that verse comfortably. One has to explain why it repeats what the other has done. The other has to explain the centuries in which the baptized were not expected to believe. And both stand downstream of Zurich, where men who confessed the same Lord and the same faith held a brother under the water for the sake of the one baptism.

*"We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life."* (Romans 6:4)

*"For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ."* (Galatians 3:27)
